title: Forgiving Word Lookup
statement:
You get a dictionary words and a list of queries. For each query, find the dictionary word it most likely meant, trying three rules in this order and stopping at the first that matches:

  1. Exact: the query is in words with exactly the same letters and case. Answer the query itself.
  2. Case slip: some word equals the query when both are lowercased. Answer the first such word in words, with its own casing.
  3. Vowel slip: some word equals the query when both are lowercased and every vowel (a e i o u) is treated as the same letter. Answer the first such word in words.

If no rule matches, the answer is the empty string "". Return the answers in query order.

examples.why: "lamp" matches exactly. "LAMP" and "lump" fall back to the first case-insensitive / vowel-insensitive word, which is "Lamp", not "lamp". "map" is a letter short.
An exact match wins even when an earlier word matches ignoring case.
Vowels may change but must stay in the same positions, and consonants never change.

hints: Three rules, each with its own notion of "the same word". Can you turn each notion into a key?
Exact match is a set lookup. For the other two, map a normalized key (lowercased; lowercased with vowels replaced by one symbol) to a word.
Store only the first word seen for each key, so later duplicates do not overwrite it. Then each query is at most three lookups.

explain.intuition:
Each rule is an equality test after normalizing both sides. Normalize the dictionary once, keyed by the normalized form, and every query becomes a few hash lookups instead of a scan of the whole list.

The only subtle part is "first such word": when you build the maps, insert a key only if it is not there yet. That is the same trick as a cache that keeps the first value it saw.
steps: Put every word into a set for exact matches.
Build lower: lowercase form → first word with that form.
Build devowel: lowercase form with each vowel replaced by * → first word with that form.
For each query, try the set, then lower, then devowel, and fall back to "".
pitfalls: Overwriting map entries, which keeps the last matching word instead of the first.
Checking the case-insensitive map before the exact set. "note" must answer "note" even if "Note" comes first.
Forgetting to lowercase before masking vowels, so uppercase vowels are not treated as vowels.

solutions.title: Scan the dictionary three times per query
solutions.idea: For each query, scan for an exact match, then a lowercase match, then a vowel-masked match.

solutions.title: Three hash lookups
solutions.idea: Precompute an exact set and two maps from normalized key to the first word with that key.

followups: Add a fourth rule: one letter may be typed wrong. How would you index the dictionary for that?
The dictionary changes while queries keep arriving. What has to change in the maps when a word is removed?
